headline: July 17 and Washington's Running a Month Ahead of Where It Should Be
subhead: The edge has been holding clean blue water since the Fourth, and the yellowfin bite out here is already doing what most years don't happen until August.
body_markdown:
I've been saying it since May — Washingts early. Every year somebody new to the canyon circuit asks me why we're already trolling spreader bars in June when Norfolk and the Baltimore boats are still waiting on their water to turn over, and every year the answer's the same: this canyon sits right where the Stream likes to throw a filament north and pin it against the shelf edge. That happened again this year, and it happened early. We're seventeen days into July and Washington is fishing like it's the second week of August. I don't say that to brag. I say it because if you've been planning your trip around the old calendar, you're behind.

The setup right now is a warm-water push that's been sitting on the 100-fathom curve since right around the holiday, holding tight along a line that runs from about 38°22'N, 74°08'W down through the canyon head and out past the 300-fathom break. That's the edge I've been working, and it's held together better than most early-season filaments do — usually these things get chewed up by a cold eddy sliding off the shelf, but this one's stayed clean. Blue water, real blue, not that green Bight soup you're fighting up around the Hudson canyons right now. That distinction matters more than people think. Clean water holds bait, bait holds tuna, and tuna hold still long enough for you to actually catch them instead of guessing.

Yellowfin have been the story. Forty to seventy pound class fish, mostly in the morning push, trolling a standard spread — Islanders and ballyhoo combos on the shotgun and long riggers, a spreader bar with the bird out front working the middle. We've had our best runs right on that 100-fathom hook where the edge kicks north, not out in open water. The fish are using the structure of the drop the same way stripers use a rip — they're stacking where the current bends and the bait gets squeezed. I had a morning last week where we marked bait balls stacked from sixty to a hundred and forty feet on the machine right over that bend, and we didn't have to leave a two-mile stretch of water to get our fish. That's not something I say lightly this early in a season — usually we're still running and gunning in mid-July, covering thirty, forty miles a day hunting temp breaks. This year the fish told us where to sit.

Bigeye have been mixed. We're getting them, but it's a night game right now — chunking and jigging the drop after dark, working depths from two hundred to four hundred feet on the sounder over the deep canyon wall. It's not a sure thing. Two out of five trips down there after dark have produced, and when it's on, it's one or two quality fish, not a double-digit night. If you're chasing bigeye specifically, I'd rather you know that going in than sell you a bill of goods.

White marlin have shown better than I expected for mid-July. We've had shots on the color change out past the canyon rim, working dink ballyhoo and small squid chains dropped back off teasers, and the fish have been eating — not every day, but enough that I'm not surprised anymore when the reel clicks off on a long rigger with no warning. Best window's been that hour before the wind fills in, when the water lies down and you can actually see the fish come up on the teaser instead of guessing from the rod tip.

Mahi have been scattered around anything floating — pots, debris, weed lines pushed up along the edge of that warm filament. Small stuff mostly, schoolies in the ten to fifteen pound range, but enough of them stacked under structure that a stop to pitch bait is worth the five minutes. Bring light spinning gear rigged with small skirted jigs or strips of squid and you can pick off a few extra fish while your spread's still soaking.

Wahoo have been the wildcard. We've pulled a couple off high-speed gear — wireline with a Wahoo Bomber style lure run fast, sixteen, eighteen knots, right on the edge where the temp break is sharpest. Not consistent, but when that filament holds tight against the shelf like it's been doing, wahoo like to sit right on that seam. Worth a couple lines in the spread if you're already out there.

Here's what I know about this canyon after enough years to stop pretending I know everything: filaments like the one we've got don't last forever. The Stream will eventually push another eddy through and either strengthen this thing or tear it apart. Right now the edge is intact, the water's clean, and the fish are using the structure exactly the way you'd draw it up on a whiteboard. If I had one day this week, I'd fish the early morning push right on that 100-fathom bend where we've been finding bait stacked, troll the standard spread, and keep bigeye gear rigged for after dark if conditions allow an overnight. If the filament holds through the weekend, I don't see a reason for this to slow down. If it slides, we adjust — that's canyon fishing. But right now, Washington's ahead of the calendar again, same as it always is, and the fish are cooperating.
